citations.quote: The DEF integrates data from multiple engineering tools into a cohesive dataset using the Violet tool, which organizes the data as a graph database aligned with the University of Arizona Ontology Stack (UAOS). We extend prior work by applying the DEF to a cubesat design project. In particular, we develop a Python-based analysis to simulate orbital decay and calculate the time required for the cubesat to deorbit.

A critical aspect of cubesat design is the ability to tie together descriptive models with analyses. The seamless integration of descriptive models, such as those defining system architecture, behavior, and requirements, with analytical tools used for simulations, trade studies, and performance evaluations can not only ensure consistency across different stages of development but also enable iterative refinement and rapid exploration of design alternatives.

The DEF has been deployed in systems engineering classrooms [13] and applied to various use cases, including digital test and evaluation [14,15], Bayesian representation of test strategies [16,17], and closed-loop orbital analysis of spacecraft [18,19].

Kaslow's CubeSat Reference Model is a notable example, providing a standardized MBSE framework specifically for modeling cubesats [36, 37]. This framework enables the representation of cubesat subsystems and interfaces in a structured, reusable manner, facilitating system-level analysis and interoperability.

MR1 Deorbit The cubesat shall deorbit within 25 years of the end of its mission. MR3 Power The cubesat shall continuously operate during its orbit. MR4 Image Resolution The cubesat shall capture images of the Earth at a resolution of 40m per pixel.

citations.quote: In this section, we describe the design and analysis of the notional Cloud Analysis and Tracking Satellite (CATSAT) mission. CATSAT is a cubesat that will be used to ascertain cloud types and monitor their movement from low-Earth orbit (LEO). As a 2U cubesat, it will be comprised of two cubesat units and will have dimensions of 20cm x 10cm x 10cm. One unit will contain the payload, a high-resolution camera. The other will contain the supporting systems and will provide functions associated with power, communication and control.

The System Architect bases the CATSAT model on the CubeSat Reference Model [37]. Fig. 2 shows how SysON has been used to model the CATSAT architecture in accordance with the CubeSat Reference Model. Note that although the Cubesat Reference Model provides a framework to model cubesats up to and including 'Cubesat Domain' (which includes external constraints, launch services, ground station services, etc.), the System Architect only models the cubesat itself. We assume that the mass of the cubesat bus (i.e., the sum of all components except the camera payload) is 1.7kg.

While the System Architect has used SysON to define the system architecture, they have also been able to reuse existing models of specific components to ease the design process. For example, consider the three options for cubesat cameras in Table 2. These components have been modeled using SysML v2 and stored in a library of cubesat cameras. When we design our cubesat, we can simply type our 'Camera' part by whichever specific camera we choose.

citations.quote: The result of the orbital decay analysis is used to verify 'MR1 - Deorbit', and is dependent on both the orbit and the cubesat design parameters (e.g., its mass, cross-sectional area, and drag coefficient). It is only possible to calculate and display this value because of the integration of these datasets, which have been collated within the DE environment. The dashboard dynamically updates this information when the inputs are changed, allowing stakeholders to explore the effects of design changes on orbital decay predictions.

If we use Camera 1 as our Payload, our total cubesat mass is 2.1kg. Our cubesat orbit is circular and has an altitude of 465km. Assuming that CATSAT has a drag coefficient of 2.2 and an area of $ 0.02 \mathrm{~m}^{2} $ (a 2U cubesat is $ 20\mathrm{cm}\times10\mathrm{cm}\times10\mathrm{cm} $ ), the orbital decay analysis calculates that it will take 22.93 years for the cubesat to deorbit, thus verifying 'MR1-Deorbit'.

These changes would be automatically reflected in the 'Orbit' tab, where the updated simulation results are displayed, and in the 'Requirements' tab, where the verification activities and results are adjusted to account for the new design parameters.

1) In SysON, change the specification that types the Payload. 2) Re-upload the cubesat architecture SysML model to Violet. Assuming the model structure is equivalent and the only differences are the attribute values, then the connections to the requirements, Python analyses, etc., will remain unaffected. Changes in the values will trigger the Python analyses to be executed in Violet. 3) In Violet, regenerate the OML representation of the project. 4) Refresh the queries in OML Rosetta. 5) Refresh the dashboard.

In this case, we can determine that while Camera 2 offers improved resolution, the resulting increase in the mass of the cubesat severely impacts the time it would take the cubesat to deorbit. It is calculated that CATSAT would have a mass of 2.4kg and it would take 26.21 years to deorbit. This is outside of the allowable limit defined in 'MR1-Deorbit'. Although Camera 1 does not provide as good a resolution as Camera 2, we can see from Fig. 7 that it still satisfies mission requirement 'MR4-Image Resolution' and so should be selected.

These dashboards have been defined in Python using the Streamlit, Graphviz and Plotly packages. To generate the data to be displayed in the dashboards, we have defined SPARQL (SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language) queries that extract particular views of the OML dataset and present them in a JSON format. The JSON output files are then ingested by the dashboards to be processed and presented.

The DEF's framework adheres to the University of Arizona Ontology Stack (UAOS), a layered ontology stack designed to ensure coherent data representation [26]. The UAOS incorporates foundational, core, and domain ontologies, reusing existing standards wherever possible. The UAOS has been written in the Ontological Modeling Language (OML).
